Definition: Whether legal or regulatory requirements obligate payment service providers to notify users, regulators, and/or data protection authorities about payment data breaches, cybersecurity incidents, or unauthorized access within specified timeframes.
Comments: No credible evidence found of mandatory personal-data breach notification requirements in Sierra Leone's general legal framework for payment/consumer data; Cyber Security and Crime Act 2021 establishes cybersecurity institutions and offences but sources reviewed did not specify mandatory breach notification to individuals/regulator; searched within the Act and related government communications for "breach notification/incident notification".

revision_notes: Originally scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A light Exa check surfaced authoritative evidence: Data Protection Africa (2022) confirms no data protection law existed in Sierra Leone at that time, and the Ministry of Information and Civic Education (April 2026) confirms Cabinet has only just approved a Data Protection Policy paving the way for a future law — i.e. no comprehensive data protection or breach-notification legislation is yet in force. The National Payment Systems Act 2022 (fetched and read in full via search excerpts) imposes consumer disclosure duties on payment service providers but no explicit breach-notification requirement. Recalculated from 0 to 1 (No) based on the absence of any in-force mandatory breach-notification law covering payment service providers.
revised_comments: Sierra Leone has no dedicated law mandating payment service providers to notify users, regulators or a data protection authority of data breaches within a specified timeframe. The Data Protection and Right to Access Information Bill, which would introduce such requirements, remained before Cabinet as at April 2026 and has not yet been enacted into law. The National Payment Systems Act 2022 imposes general consumer disclosure obligations on payment service providers but does not include a specific breach-notification duty.

Definition: Whether payment system governance explicitly includes mechanisms to ensure inclusivity and represent interests of vulnerable populations, including provisions for input from all participant types, consumer representatives, small providers, or explicit financial inclusion mandates in governance documents.
Comments: No credible public evidence found of formal pro-poor governance mechanisms (e.g., mandated consumer/CSO representation in payment scheme governance bodies) for the National Payment Switch/Instant Payment Service; searched for "governance", "committee", "representation", "financial inclusion governance" related to BSL switch and NPSA.

revision_notes: Originally scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A light Exa check surfaced the National Payment Systems Act 2022, which establishes a National Payment System Committee including mobile money operators, community banks (via the Apex Bank) and the Fintech Association, and imposes a statutory duty on the Central Bank to extend financial services beyond traditional branch-based channels. The Bank of Sierra Leone's National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2022-2026 further sets explicit targets for women, youth, rural communities and MSMEs. Recalculated from 0 to 2 (Partial): inclusion-oriented mechanisms exist in law and strategy, but there is no dedicated consumer or vulnerable-population representative seat written into the payment scheme's own governance charter.
revised_comments: Payment system governance in Sierra Leone includes some inclusion-oriented mechanisms rather than a comprehensive pro-poor governance framework. The National Payment Systems Act 2022 establishes a National Payment System Committee with representation from mobile money operators, community banks (via the Apex Bank) and the Fintech Association, alongside a statutory duty on the Central Bank to extend financial services beyond traditional branch-based channels. The Bank of Sierra Leone's National Strategy for Financial Inclusion 2022-2026 sets targets for women, youth, rural communities and MSMEs, though this sits alongside rather than within the payment scheme's formal governance charter.

Comments: Could not find publicly available scheme rules/rulebook for the National Payment Switch/Instant Payment Service; official BSL site was inaccessible to automated browsing (robots restriction), and secondary sources did not link to a public rulebook; therefore scored as unknown.

No single consolidated public rulebook URL was located during this check, so the exact tier (on-request vs fully public) is uncertain. Recalculated from 0 to 2 (Partial — available via Gazette/on request), flagged for human review to confirm whether a downloadable rulebook exists on the BSL website.
revised_comments: Rules governing Sierra Leone's national payment switch and instant payment service are issued as Central Bank directives, such as the National Switch Directives 2023, which under the National Payment Systems Act 2022 must be published in the Gazette or on the Bank's website at least fifteen days before taking effect. Specific clauses of these directives have been quoted and reported by local media, indicating they are accessible on request or through official publication, though no single consolidated public rulebook document has been located.

Comments: No credible evidence found of specific policies or payment-programme accommodations enabling refugees/migrants to access digital payments (e.g., refugee KYC exceptions, UNHCR-linked mobile money programs) in Sierra Leone; searched for UNHCR, refugee, migrant, KYC, mobile money Sierra Leone.

revision_notes: Originally scored 0/Unknown with no source cited. A light Exa check surfaced a clearly authoritative source: an August 2024 partnership between Orange Money and the International Organization for Migration specifically to channel payments to migrants (including internally displaced persons and migrant workers) through Orange Money's mobile money platform, plus a UNDP/UNCDF digital financial services assessment showing that a valid passport is among the accepted KYC/CDD documents for opening a mobile money account. Recalculated from 0 to 2 (Partial), reflecting a practical access pathway via mobile money for non-nationals holding a passport, though formal AML/KYC documentation requirements may still exclude undocumented or stateless individuals.
revised_comments: Refugees, migrants and other non-nationals in Sierra Leone can access digital payment accounts in practice, primarily through mobile money. Orange Money and the International Organization for Migration signed a partnership in August 2024 to channel payments to migrants, including internally displaced persons and migrant workers, through the Orange Money platform. Customer due diligence requirements for opening a mobile money account accept a range of identity documents, including a valid passport, providing a pathway for non-nationals, though formal KYC/AML requirements can still present barriers for undocumented or stateless individuals.
